result: Using STORM imaging, the authors revealed a laminar organization of ECM proteins within the GBM, showing that agrin, laminin-521, and collagen IV have highly oriented macromolecular organization with specific spatial distributions. The study demonstrated that agrin and laminin-521 each form two layers with their C-terminal domains near cell membranes and N-terminal domains toward the GBM interior, while collagen α3α4α5(IV) localizes centrally and collagen α1α1α2(IV) localizes near the endothelial side.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praised this work, stating 'This manuscript provides novel insights into the organization of ECM in kidney glomerular basement membrane' and 'Overall this is a very well executed study with data of very high quality.' The reviewers acknowledged that the authors 'show that the ECM in these cells is much more organized than generally believed,' directly supporting the core findings about laminar organization and protein distributions.

result: The authors optimized the Tokuyasu method for STORM imaging and developed a molecular reference frame using agrinC as an internal standard, with agrinC positions at ±68.9 nm from the GBM center. This methodology was validated by showing nearly identical results with two different agrinC antibodies and consistent positioning when using different reference proteins.
evaluation: While reviewers praised the use of the Tokuyasu protocol as 'a very nice aspect of this study,' they requested validation using different fixation methods, noting that 'the measurements obtained are unlikely to be absolute (they are, however, excellent in terms of relative spatial positioning).' Reviewers also requested clarification of the geometry of analysis and how localizations were defined, indicating methodological concerns that need addressing.

result: The authors claim that the GBM's laminin component is divided into two networks, one produced by podocytes and the other by endothelial cells, with limited mobility of laminin trimers across the GBM thickness. This interpretation is based on transgenic mice expressing human laminin α5 and showing that laminin from each cell type remains on its respective side.
evaluation: Reviewer 8 directly challenged this interpretation, stating 'their labelling of endogenous Laminin indicates just one central Laminin-rich region and their claim for two networks depends on data derived from the ectopic expression of human Laminin α5.' The reviewer noted 'This interpretation needs to be refined,' indicating that the evidence for two separate networks is not conclusive based on endogenous labeling alone.

result: The authors extended their analysis to human GBM, showing that it is approximately twice as thick as mouse GBM (~400 nm vs ~200 nm) with similar laminar organization. They found that the increased thickness is attributed to an expanded collagen α3α4α5(IV) network and an additional layer of LM-521, with collagen α1α1α2(IV) occupying space between the central collagen α3α4α5(IV) layer and the endothelial surface.
evaluation: Reviewer 9 identified a significant discrepancy, noting that 'AgrinC is much richer on the podocyte face and almost absent from the capillary side' in Figure 5B, contradicting the authors' description that 'AgrinC and integrin β1 are described as being localized along the endothelial and podocyte surfaces of the human GBM.' The reviewer stated 'This discrepancy between the results presented and the text needs to be addressed,' indicating uncertainty about the accuracy of the human GBM characterization.

result: In a mouse model of Alport syndrome lacking collagen α3α4α5(IV), the authors observed disruptions in GBM architecture including thin GBM regions with intact 2-layered agrin, breakdown of agrin layering, thick irregular GBM stretches with disorganized agrin, and atypical distribution of collagen α1α1α2(IV) spread across the GBM width.
evaluation: Reviewers did not raise specific concerns about the Alport syndrome findings. The overall positive assessment of the study as 'very well executed' and having 'data of very high quality' implicitly supports these disease model observations, which demonstrate the utility of the STORM approach for detecting pathological changes in GBM architecture.

result: The authors found that collagen α3α4α5(IV) N- and C-terminal domains map to the center of the GBM, too distant from integrin β1 for meaningful ligand-receptor interaction in human GBM. They conclude that agrinC and laminin α5-LG are the likely biologically relevant integrin β1 ligands, while collagen α1α1α2(IV) at the endothelial side is near enough to bind integrin β1.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these interpretations about ligand-receptor interactions. The statement that this was 'one of our most important and unexpected findings' aligns with reviewers' acknowledgment that the study provides 'novel insights' and shows ECM is 'much more organized than generally believed,' supporting the significance and validity of these spatial relationship findings.

result: The authors justify their use of STORM by citing that super-resolution microscopy methods have broken the diffraction limit and have been successfully applied to dissect nanoscale architecture of multi-protein complexes in various cellular structures.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 requested that the authors 'Explain more clearly why 3D-SIM and/or STED are not be suitable for imaging 200 nm sections' and suggested they 'consider validating some of their key results using another imaging method, like 3D-SIM and STED (and GFP fusion proteins).' This indicates the reviewers were not fully convinced that STORM was the only appropriate method and wanted justification for the methodological choice.
